subject: iot
title: Unit 4 — Attack Surface, Zero Trust, Firmware & PKI MCQs

items.q: Why is the IoT attack surface considered uniquely broad?
options: It spans physical devices, networks, and cloud simultaneously — and is only as strong as the weakest layer
IoT devices cannot be attacked physically
items.explain: IoT can be attacked by holding the device (physical), sniffing its radio (network), or breaching its cloud API — so defenders must secure every layer, not just one.

items.q: The OWASP IoT Top 10 is best described as:
options: A ranking of the 10 most secure IoT devices
A community checklist of the most common, impactful IoT vulnerabilities to fix
A list of approved IoT vendors
items.explain: The OWASP IoT Top 10 is a practical, beginner-friendly checklist of the most common and impactful IoT weaknesses to prioritize — not a product ranking.

items.q: Which vulnerability tops the OWASP IoT Top 10 and enabled the Mirai botnet?
items.explain: Weak/guessable/hardcoded passwords are OWASP IoT #1 — default credentials let Mirai conscript cameras and gateways into a DDoS botnet.

items.q: Which OWASP IoT issue directly explains why the LockState/Jeep firmware problems were so severe?
options: Lack of a secure update mechanism
items.explain: Lack of a secure (signed, reliable) update mechanism (OWASP #4) means devices can't be safely patched — a buggy/unsigned update can brick or compromise them, as with LockState and the Jeep hack.

items.q: What is the core principle of Zero Trust?
options: 'Never Trust, Always Verify' — authenticate and authorize every request regardless of network location
Build a single strong perimeter and trust the interior
items.explain: Zero Trust assumes no implicit trust based on location; every request (inside or outside) is verified explicitly, with least-privilege access and an assume-breach mindset.

items.q: What is the fatal flaw of traditional perimeter-based ('castle-and-moat') security for IoT?
options: Once an attacker breaches the perimeter, the trusted interior lets them roam freely — and IoT has many weak endpoints to breach
It cannot connect to the internet
items.explain: Perimeter security trusts everything inside, so a single breached device (a hacked bulb, a phished laptop) gives an attacker free lateral movement — untenable with countless weak IoT endpoints.

items.q: Zero Trust replaces network-based security with identity-based security, meaning trust is based on:
options: Which network/VLAN you are connected to
Cryptographically verified identity, proven on every request
How long the device has been online
items.explain: Network-based security asks 'are you on the trusted network?' (spoofable, useless once inside). Identity-based security asks 'can you prove who you are?' — every time. Zero Trust uses who you are, not where you are.

items.q: Which device-authentication method is the strongest among these for Zero Trust?
options: Certificate-based (X.509) identity, ideally with a hardware root of trust
items.explain: Certificate-based (X.509) identity — especially with keys in a hardware secure element/TPM — provides strong cryptographic device authentication, far better than shared or hardcoded passwords.

items.q: What is the purpose of Binwalk in IoT security?
options: It analyzes and extracts the contents of a firmware image (bootloader, kernel, filesystem) by scanning for signatures
items.explain: Binwalk scans a firmware binary for signatures of embedded components and extracts/decompresses the filesystem, letting analysts (attackers AND defenders) inspect it for secrets and vulnerabilities.

items.q: Why is finding a hardcoded credential or private key in firmware especially dangerous?
options: Every device of that model typically shares it — extract it once and you can potentially compromise the entire fleet
items.explain: Hardcoded secrets are usually identical across all units of a model, so extracting one from a single device can unlock the whole fleet — a serious, repeated IoT failure (OWASP #1).

items.q: What is the main DEFENSIVE lesson from firmware analysis being possible?
options: Assume firmware is extractable: never hardcode secrets, encrypt + sign firmware (secure boot), and use a hardware root of trust
items.explain: Because firmware can be extracted and inspected, secure design assumes it will be: no plaintext secrets, encrypted and signed firmware with secure boot, signed OTA updates, and keys in a hardware secure element.

items.q: What does an X.509 certificate fundamentally provide?
options: It binds a public key to an identity, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) — a cryptographic 'ID card'
It is a type of battery
items.explain: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to a subject's identity and is signed by a CA, so others can trust that the public key really belongs to that device/server.

items.q: How is a digital signature created?
options: By encrypting the data with the recipient's public key
By hashing the data and encrypting the hash with the signer's private key (verified with the signer's public key)
items.explain: The signer hashes the data and encrypts the hash with their private key. Anyone can verify with the public key — giving authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation. A CA signs certificates this way.

items.q: In the chain of trust, how is a device certificate ultimately trusted?
options: By trusting any certificate it presents
By verifying signatures up the chain (device → intermediate CA → root CA) to a root you already trust
items.explain: Trust flows from a self-signed Root CA → Intermediate CAs → device certificate. Verification walks UP the chain to a trusted root (in your trust store). Break any link and identity can't be verified.

options: The system of CAs, policies, and procedures that issue, manage, validate, and revoke certificates
items.explain: PKI is the framework (CAs, registration authorities, revocation via CRL/OCSP) that makes certificates trustworthy at scale — issuing, managing, and revoking them.

items.q: Why is certificate-based (mutual TLS) authentication ideal for IoT and Zero Trust?
options: It is the same as a shared password
It gives strong cryptographic device identity (both sides prove identity), far better than shared passwords — and underpins 'verify identity, not network'
It removes the need for any keys
It only works without the internet
items.explain: Certificate-based identity (mutual TLS, where device and server both present certificates) is the strongest practical device authentication, used by AWS IoT/Azure, and the foundation of Zero Trust's identity-first model.
